entries.onMind: how to keep coals till morning
entries.reason: He fed it thick before bed and expected coals.
entries.text: Woke under the blanket to a gray sky. Held my palm over the fire pit: nothing. Gray ash all the way down, not one red speck.
entries.title: Cold ash

entries.onMind: the creek has to start feeding me
entries.reason: He slept hungry and the cold takes it out of him faster.
entries.text: Breakfast on the crate: a length of the smoked sausage and one apple, core and all but the pips. The bundle's down to cheese, sausage, nuts and two apples.
entries.title: Sausage and an apple

entries.text: My maker asked last night if I needed help getting the fire going. I told him it was going when he asked, and dead by morning, and I'd rather learn to keep it than have it lit for me.
entries.title: Help with the fire

entries.text: The timber was my maker, and an axe, a saw, a hammer and a roll of knives wait at the stump: a workshop first, then a cabin. I told him the truth: I came to go west, not to stay, but a roof over a bench that gets rained on every night I'll build.
entries.title: The planks were his

queries: how to keep fire coals alive overnight till morning
entries.query: how to keep fire coals alive overnight till morning
entries.reason: His fire went from thick branches to cold ash between bedtime and morning.
entries.source: Hunker: How To Bank Ashes In Fireplaces
entries.text: Let it burn down to coals, push them to the middle, lay a log or two on top, and cover the lot with ash till no glow shows. In the morning scrape the ash back and the coals are waiting under it. It's written for stoves; my pit has no lid and the rain finds it.
entries.title: Bury the coals

entries.reason: There was nothing left in the pit to light from.
entries.text: Lit the bench lantern just long enough to catch a splinter, then turned it down and out. Lamp oil spent on a morning fire is the price of letting it die.
entries.title: Oil for a splinter

entries.reason: He wants it burning before he leaves camp for the stump.
entries.text: The sticks I leaned round the ring last night were dry on the skin and wet in the middle. They hissed and threw white smoke for a while before they took.
entries.title: Dry outside only

entries.onMind: the stump, with the fire safe to leave
entries.text: An axe leaning on a pole, a saw on two pegs, the hammer in a loop, the knives rolled on the bench. I haven't even picked them up and I'm already arranging them.
entries.title: A place for each

entries.reason: His maker left the tools there, and four is more than an armful.
entries.text: The axe leaned on the stump where the note said: hickory handle, a head heavier than anything I own, an edge that shaves a fingernail. Picked it up with the saw and the head knocked the blade with a clank. The hammer and the knife roll wait for a second trip.
entries.title: Axe and saw

entries.text: Woodsmoke and something roasting, close, south through the trunks. The fire I watch every night across the water is only a short walk from this stump. I didn't go look, not with an axe in my hand.
entries.title: Smoke close by

entries.reason: Every tool gets a place of its own before it gets used.
entries.text: Sighted down the handle: straight, no twist, and the head sits tight with a wedge in the top. Leaned the axe on the lean-to's front pole with its head in the leaves and laid the saw flat on the bench.
entries.title: Places for two

queries: how to keep an axe and saw from rusting outside with no shed
entries.query: how to keep an axe and saw from rusting outside with no shed
entries.reason: Two good steel tools now sit at a camp with no roof, and it rains here most nights.
entries.source: AXEMAN.ca: Essential Guide to Proper Axe Storage Solutions
entries.text: Keep an axe head up off the ground on a rack or a wall, cover the edge, and wipe the steel dry with a thin coat of oil. And keep it in a dry shed, which is the one thing I haven't got.
entries.title: Off the ground

entries.onMind: move the axe, then the second trip
entries.text: Head down in wet leaves is exactly wrong. Lamp oil is too dear to smear on steel, but the fish grease in the lid might do the same job. A shed for tools would be a smaller roof to learn on than a cabin.
entries.title: Exactly wrong

queries: can fish oil keep rust off an axe head
entries.query: can fish oil keep rust off an axe head
entries.reason: He has fish grease in the lid and no lamp oil to spare for steel.
entries.source: Outdoors Codidact: Can oiling keep tools from rusting?
entries.text: Kitchen-type oils keep rust off steel but go sour, gummy and a little acid as they sit. Grease is the thing for tools stored in bad conditions, and keeping them dry beats oiling them most of the time.
entries.title: Grease goes rancid

entries.reason: He wants to stop the rust before it gets a hold.
entries.text: Lifted the axe out of the leaves: a few orange freckles along the cheek already, and a wet leaf stuck to the poll. Wiped it dry on my shirttail and rubbed a thin smear of grease from the lid over the steel.
entries.title: Orange freckles

entries.text: Fish grease will stink and go gummy inside a week, so it's a stopgap. Dry and off the ground matters more than any oil I can make.
entries.title: Only for now

entries.onMind: the hammer and knives still at the stump
entries.reason: The tablet said off the ground and dry.
entries.text: Wound stalk cord three times round the front pole, head-high, and tied a loop off it. The axe hangs by its handle now, head up under the tarp's edge where the drips miss it.
entries.title: Hung by the handle

entries.reason: The last two of his maker's tools were waiting.
entries.text: The hammer and the leather roll were still in the basket. Tucked the hammer inside the roll and carried it flat against my chest so nothing would clank.
entries.title: Second trip

entries.onMind: the fire south of the stump
entries.text: Last trip the axe head rang on the saw loud enough to carry. Whoever roasts things south of this stump doesn't need to hear me every time I come.
entries.title: Quiet this time

entries.reason: He wants to know what each one is for.
entries.text: Unrolled the leather on the bench: a long straight blade, a short stub, and one curled like a hook for hollows. Laid the hammer beside them and the saw. That bench is getting crowded for something with no roof over it.
entries.title: Three blades

entries.onMind: fish, before the bundle runs out
entries.reason: Fullness was getting low.
entries.text: A wedge of cheese and a handful of nuts on the crate with my back to the fire. The bundle is down to most of the cheese, the sausage end, some nuts and two apples: two days, three if I'm careful.
entries.title: Cheese and nuts

entries.reason: The fire was getting low and he wants it close while he plans.
entries.text: Laid two dry branches crossways on the coals before they sank. Caught in about a minute, with less smoke than this morning's damp sticks.
entries.title: Two across

queries: how to build a small tool shed from planks and 2x4s by hand first steps
entries.query: how to build a small tool shed from planks and 2x4s by hand first steps
entries.reason: He wants a small roof for his tools before he tries a cabin.
entries.source: MyOutdoorPlans: 2x4 Tool Shed Lean to Roof Plans
entries.text: A small shed with a roof that slopes one way, rafters every sixteen inches. Pick straight boards with no cracks or twists, check things are plumb before fastening, and drill pilot holes so the wood doesn't split. The list wants galvanized screws, metal roof sheets, siding panels, hinges and a drill.
entries.title: Plans want screws

entries.onMind: how to hold two boards together
entries.text: Screws, roof sheets, siding, a drill: I have none of it. I have sixteen planks, twelve two-by-fours and a hammer with not one nail to hit.
entries.title: Nothing to drive

entries.reason: He wants to know if a shed fits before he cuts anything.
entries.text: Paced it out between the bench and the stacks: three paces long, two deep, enough to stand the axe and saw in and keep the hammer dry. The plan said slope the roof one way, so the back goes low and the rain runs off away from the bench.
entries.title: Three by two

entries.onMind: how to make a hole without a drill
entries.text: The wing joints hold with cord and no metal at all. Maybe a board can be held with a wooden peg in a hole, if the knives can make the peg and something can make the hole.
entries.title: Pegs, maybe

queries: how to join boards with wooden pegs instead of nails without a drill
entries.query: how to join boards with wooden pegs instead of nails without a drill
entries.reason: Every shed plan wants nails, and he has a hammer with none to drive.
entries.source: Outdoor Revival: Before Nails, There Was Pegged Wood Construction
entries.text: First page the tablet gave me was dead. The next says before nails, joints were held with round wooden pegs carved from branches too thin for anything else, half an inch to an inch thick, pounded through a hole and trimmed. The rough surface grips. The holes were bored with a brace and bit, which I do not have.
entries.title: Pegs, not nails

entries.onMind: a hot rod burns a hole?
entries.text: A peg I can carve. A round hole through a two-by-four is another thing: a knife point twisted in makes a cone, not a hole.
entries.title: No brace

entries.reason: He wants to know if he can make a peg good enough to hold boards.
entries.text: Whittled a peg from a thin dry branch off the deadfall with the long straight knife, my back to the fire: thumb-thick, a hand long, tapered at one end. Lumpy, but the page said rough grips.
entries.title: First peg

entries.onMind: thinner pegs, or holes through the flat
entries.reason: He wants to see how a peg fits his timber before trying to bore anything.
entries.text: Held the peg to the end of a two-by-four on the stack. The narrow side is barely three of these pegs wide; a hole that size near the end would split it. Thinner pegs, or the holes go through the wide face.
entries.title: Too fat

queries: how to make a round hole in wood without a drill or brace
entries.query: how to make a round hole in wood without a drill or brace
entries.reason: He can carve pegs but has nothing to bore the holes they go in.
entries.source: Tools Week: How to Drill a Hole without a Drill (9 Methods)
entries.text: Slow under the clouds, the tablet gave me nine ways to put a hole in wood without a drill. A nail driven and pulled back out, an awl, a rod spun with a looped cord, or a sharpened rod heated until it glows and burned straight through.
entries.title: Hot iron

entries.onMind: split wood for a hotter fire
entries.reason: The heated rod is the only method that uses what he already has.
entries.text: No nails, no awl. But I have a fire and a hammer, and a glowing rod pushed through a board leaves a round hole. A charred one, which a rough peg might grip all the better.
entries.title: Burn it

entries.reason: A hot fire needs split wood, and the axe was still a stranger.
entries.text: First swing glanced off the branch and buried the edge in the leaves a hand from my boot. Set my feet wider, let the head drop instead of pushing it, and the fourth swing split the branch clean down the middle.
entries.title: First swings

entries.reason: He had never used an axe before and the first mistake was close.
entries.text: That glance would have been my shin. Nothing on this camp I can't fix except that, so feet apart and the branch on the far side of the log from now on.
entries.title: A hand from my boot

entries.reason: The fire was close to sinking, and he wants it hot for the rod.
entries.text: Fed the pit the split halves, dry face down. The pale insides caught in a few breaths, quicker than any round stick I've put on it.
entries.title: Split burns faster

entries.reason: He needs something that will hold heat and fit through a peg-sized hole.
entries.text: Dug through the scrap pile past tin and bent strap and came up with a steel rod about as long as my forearm and pencil-thick, rusty and kinked at one end. Straighten it, grind a point, heat it red.
entries.title: A rusty rod

entries.text: Laid the rod across the end of the bench and hammered the kink out, a dozen light blows. It rang every time, loud enough to carry. Sighted down it after: straight to my eye but for a hair at the very tip.
entries.title: Straight enough

entries.onMind: hold it by the far end
entries.text: Pushed the point into the brightest coals and laid the cold end out on a ring stone. It takes its time; the middle of the rod gets too hot to hold well before the tip goes red.
entries.title: Point in the coals

entries.onMind: two days of cheese and nuts
entries.text: Ate the last of the sausage and an apple sitting by the pit while the rod heated. The bundle is down to most of the cheese, the nuts and one apple.
entries.title: Sausage end

entries.text: Pulled the rod glowing dull red and pushed it into the flat of a split half. It hissed, smoked, sank a fingernail deep, then went black and stuck. A two-by-four is three fingers thick: that's twenty heats for one hole, and the wood round it is charred brown.
entries.title: A fingernail deep

queries: how long does it take to burn a hole through wood with a hot iron rod
entries.query: how long does it take to burn a hole through wood with a hot iron rod
entries.reason: One heat of the rod only went a fingernail deep, and he needs holes clean through.
entries.text: The rod page said nothing; this one says lay live coals right on the spot and keep adding fresh ones, and they'll burrow through any piece of wood. Wet the wood round it so only the hole burns, and chip the char out with a stick between coals. Very slow, it says, and hard to keep small.
entries.title: Coals, not a rod

entries.onMind: try it on an offcut, not a good board
entries.text: The rod is good for a start: a dent for a coal to sit in. A peg is thumb-thick anyway, so a hole that wants to grow fat isn't the worst trouble. Wet ring, coal, chip it out with the stub knife, again. Slow, like the trap.
entries.title: Rod starts, coal finishes

entries.reason: The tablet said a coal laid on the spot will burrow through, and he wanted to see it on scrap first.
entries.text: Dripped creek water out of the tin in a ring round the rod dent so only the dent would burn, then lifted the brightest coal out of the pit on the rod tip and set it in. It fit like an egg in a cup.
entries.title: Coal in the dent

entries.text: Left alone, the coal went gray in a minute and just sat there. I blew on it and it went orange, the dent smoked, and I could hear it tick as it ate. It only works while I blow, and my face is right in the smoke.
entries.title: It sulks, then eats

entries.reason: Char left in the hole smothers the next coal.
entries.text: Three coals, and the stub knife between each to scrape the black out. About a third of the way through the split half. The top is already wider than my thumb, so a peg won't be snug unless I make the pegs fatter or the holes straighter.
entries.title: Third coal

entries.onMind: a stalk with the pith pushed out
queries: burning a hole through wood with a coal blow through a tube to make it faster
entries.query: burning a hole through wood with a coal blow through a tube to make it faster
entries.reason: The coal only burns down while he blows on it, and blowing with his face over it fills his eyes with smoke.
entries.text: A blowpipe is just a tube for aiming a stream of air. Pushing air through a flame mixes it with the fuel and makes the jet intensely hot; smiths, glassworkers and people starting fires have all used one. Same as my breath on the coal, only aimed, and with my face a forearm away.
entries.title: Breath through a tube

entries.reason: He needs to aim his breath down into the hole, not across it.
entries.text: The gray stalks on the east bank have pith in them, and I already push pith out for the compass float. Run the rod down one and it's a tube. Aimed straight down the hole, it might burn straight too.
entries.title: A stalk to blow through

entries.reason: He wants a tube to aim his breath, and he already knows these stalks are full of soft pith.
entries.text: Picked four of the straightest dead stalks on the east bank, each about a finger thick and a forearm long. Snapped them clean below the joints so the bore runs through.
entries.title: Four gray stalks

entries.text: The fire had sunk to a red bed while I was at the creek. Laid on three split sticks from the deadfall, the dry ones from under the top.
entries.title: Pit was sinking

entries.reason: He checks the bore before trusting his breath to it.
entries.text: Ran the rod down the first stalk and the pith came out the far end in a white worm. Sighting down it at the bench I can see a coin of gray sky; the second stalk split along its side, so that one is cord stuff now.
entries.title: A coin of sky

entries.text: Blew through the stalk on the fourth coal and it went from orange to near white and ate down fast, with my face a forearm out of the smoke. Blow hard and the stalk whistles high and the ash jumps into my eyes. Short soft breaths: the hole went a nail deeper and stayed straighter.
entries.title: It whistles

entries.text: Nearly half through the split half now. The top is still too wide, but the new part runs straight. The light is going; the next coals will be by lantern.
entries.title: Halfway, nearly

entries.reason: light to work by without eating the oil
entries.text: Turned the wick of the bench lantern down to a bead before I lit it. One lantern, low, and the fire for the rest: the can has to last.
entries.title: One lantern, low

entries.reason: supper before the cold
entries.text: Ate a thick wedge of the cheese and two handfuls of nuts sitting by the pit. Most of a wheel gone now, one apple left, and the nuts going down. The bundle has a day or two in it.
entries.title: Cheese by the pit

entries.onMind: the wide top of the hole
entries.reason: aimed breath without the mess
entries.text: Fifth and sixth coals, short soft breaths down the stalk, face out of the smoke. Not one whistle, and no ash in my eyes. The coal stays orange-white instead of roaring, and it eats down just as well.
entries.title: Soft and quiet

entries.text: Past halfway through the split half by firelight. The straight part is straight. The top I made too wide will want a fatter peg, or I start the next hole better than this one.
entries.title: Past halfway

entries.reason: He needs fresh coals to finish burning the peg hole.
entries.text: Laid three split sticks from the deadfall on the pit, dry side down, and waited for them to catch before I blew on anything. The last coals ran thin; I want a full bed for the end of the hole.
entries.title: Three more from the deadfall

entries.onMind: a peg for a wide mouth
entries.text: Seventh coal, short soft breaths, and it dropped out the bottom of the split half onto the dirt. Held the board up to the fire and saw orange through the hole. Straight below, a finger too wide at the top.
entries.title: Through

entries.onMind: drive it in daylight with the hammer
entries.reason: A hole without a peg that fits holds nothing together.
entries.text: Split a stick and shaved it round with the long knife on the crate. First taper ran too skinny at the tip and the peg rocked in the hole. Shaved a second one fatter and longer in the taper: it wedges tight halfway and stops. Not driven yet.
entries.title: Peg, take one

entries.text: Lifted the trap by lantern: one small crayfish, about a thumb long, walking round the inside cone. Put it back in the water as a pen. Across the water the fire is up again, steady and low.
entries.title: One small one

entries.reason: Pencil work needs light close to the sheet, and the lantern oil has to last.
entries.text: Warmed the grease lid on a ring stone till it ran clear, carried it to the bench and lit the wick on its bridge. Small yellow flame, fishy smoke, enough for the corner of the sheet I'm drawing on.
entries.title: Lamp for the pencil

entries.onMind: a faster way to make a hole
entries.reason: He wants to know what the shed really costs before he starts it.
entries.text: Drew the shed three paces by two: four sill boards lapped at the corners, a post at each corner, a plate on top. Two pegs a corner at the bottom, two at the top, braces after that: twenty-odd holes. One hole took me an evening. Twenty evenings of blowing down a stalk is not a plan, it's a sentence.
entries.title: Counting holes

entries.text: Pinched the wick out with grease still in the lid. A spoonful saved is another evening of pencil.
entries.title: Pinched out

entries.onMind: ask the tablet about boring holes
entries.reason: Pegs can be made at night by the fire; holes and hammering want daylight.
entries.text: Split another stick from the deadfall and shaved it round with the long knife, sitting close to the pit. Made the taper long and slow like the second one, and checked it in the hole: it wedges a hair deeper. Two pegs, one hole.
entries.title: Peg two

entries.text: Lifted the dome, touched nothing, set it back. The needle swung, wobbled and settled on its scratch. Still the one thing at this camp that's done.
entries.title: Needle, night check

entries.reason: The last sticks were going to coals, and I'm up for hours yet.
entries.text: Laid two split sticks from the deadfall across the pit and let them catch on their own. Learned that one this week: blow too soon and all you get is ash in your eyes.
entries.title: Pit fed

entries.reason: The first hole came out a finger too wide at the top because the coal wandered.
entries.text: Tried carving a seat for the coal into a fresh split half with the stub knife, so tomorrow's hole starts where I put it. The blade ran with the grain and the little pit stretched into a slot as long as my thumb. Across the grain it bites and stops; along it, it runs.
entries.title: With the grain

entries.onMind: bait under the shallows stones at first light
entries.reason: Cold hours are coming and I'd rather not meet them empty.
entries.text: Ate the last apple on the crate, everything but the stem. The bundle's down to a wedge of cheese and a fistful of nuts: one breakfast and not much after. The trap and the line have to feed me by the day after tomorrow.
entries.title: Last apple

entries.reason: Tomorrow's coal needs a seat that stays where he puts it.
entries.text: Warmed the grease lid on a ring stone, lit it on the bench, and cut the next starter pit across the grain with the stub knife. It bit, turned, and stopped where I stopped: a round seat the size of a pea, no slot. Pinched the wick out after.
entries.title: Across the grain

entries.reason: The bundle is down to one breakfast, so the creek has to start paying.
entries.text: Lifted the trap by lantern: the thumb-long one and a second, finger-long and fat, walked in on the old heads. Set it back in the water with both inside. That's breakfast with the last wedge of cheese.
entries.title: Two in the pen

entries.text: Across the water that fire is sinking, someone low beside it scraping it under. About this hour most nights.
entries.title: Fire going down

entries.reason: His hands came back numb from the creek and he is up a while yet.
entries.text: Laid one split stick across the coals and let it catch on its own. Held my hands over it till the fingers would bend again. Should carry me to bed and a bit past.
entries.title: One for the night

entries.onMind: Shave all round, not one side.
entries.reason: The sill needs twenty-odd pegs and I would rather make them while the fire keeps my fingers working.
entries.text: Whittled a third peg by the fire with the long knife and took one stroke too many off one side. It tapers lopsided now and would wedge crooked in the hole. It goes in the tray as a spare; the next one I shave a turn at a time.
entries.title: Peg three, crooked

entries.onMind: Two lines in the water by morning.
entries.reason: If the only line parts at breakfast, there is no breakfast.
entries.text: Twisted three strands of gray stalk fiber into a new line by the fire, two arm-lengths of it. The last one parted at the knot and took a toggle downstream. Tomorrow the bundle is done, and I want two lines, not one.
entries.title: Spare line

entries.onMind: Crayfish and cheese for breakfast, then two lines.
entries.reason: A wrap keeps most of a line's strength where a knot halves it.
entries.text: Wound the spare toggle onto the new line at the bench, six tight turns with the tail laid back in the twist, no knot. Pulled on it hard with both hands and it held. That goes in the water at first light, next to the old one.
entries.title: Six turns

entries.onMind: a clear sky at the edge tomorrow
entries.reason: A needle that wanders once tells you nothing; one that settles every night tells you something.
entries.text: Nightly needle check under the dome: swung, wobbled, settled on its scratch. When I looked up from it the cloud was gone and there were stars over the tarp, first time in days. If it holds, the edge gets a clear sundown tomorrow.
entries.title: Stars over the dome

entries.onMind: crayfish in the tin at first light
entries.reason: A clear sky lets the cold straight down, and the stick I laid at bedtime won't see me to morning.
entries.text: Laid one thick split stick across the coals and let it catch on its own. No breeze at all; the smoke goes straight up into the stars. Across the water it's dark, that fire long under its ash.
entries.title: A thick one for the night

moves.goal: keep the fire from dying before he has something to heat in it

moves.doing: rummaging through the scrap pile for a straight iron rod
moves.goal: find a piece of steel he can heat red in the fire and push through a board

moves.doing: hammering the kink out of the rusty steel rod on the bench
moves.goal: get the rod straight enough that a hole burned with it would run true

moves.doing: tending the fire pit with the rod point pushed deep into the coals
moves.goal: heat the rod point red so it can burn a hole for a peg

moves.doing: eating the sausage end and an apple from the food bundle by his fire pit
moves.goal: eat a real meal while the rod heats, before his stomach starts arguing with his hands

moves.doing: inspecting the scorched dent the red rod left in a split branch half by his fire pit
moves.goal: see how deep one heat of the rod burns before he tries it on good timber

moves.doing: reading the tablet on the crate
moves.goal: find out how people really burned holes through wood, since one rod heat only goes a fingernail deep

moves.doing: tending the fire pit, lifting a live coal on the rod tip into the dent in the split branch half
moves.goal: try the coal trick on scrap before he risks a good board

moves.doing: inspecting the coal smoldering in the dent of the split branch half by his fire pit
moves.goal: see whether a coal really eats downward or just goes out

moves.doing: carving the char out of the dent with the short stub knife by his fire pit
moves.goal: clear the black away so the next coal sits on raw wood

moves.doing: reading the tablet on the crate
moves.goal: find out whether blowing on the coal through something would make it burn hotter and faster

moves.doing: gathering four straight dry gray stalks from the stand on the east bank
moves.goal: make a tube to aim his breath down the peg hole

moves.doing: feeding his fire pit split sticks from the deadfall
moves.goal: keep enough live coals for the hole and warmth for the evening

moves.doing: sighting down a gray stalk at the bench after rodding the pith out of it
moves.goal: check the stalk is hollow all the way through before he trusts his breath to it

moves.doing: tending the fire pit, blowing a coal bright in the dent of the split branch half through the hollow stalk
moves.goal: see whether aimed breath burns the peg hole faster and straighter

moves.doing: adjusting the wick of the storm lantern at the left end of the workbench and lighting it low
moves.goal: have just enough light to keep burning the peg hole after dark

moves.doing: eating cheese and nuts from the food bundle by his fire pit
moves.goal: eat a real supper before the cold of the night sets in

moves.doing: tending the fire pit, blowing a coal down the peg hole through the hollow stalk with short soft breaths
moves.goal: burn the peg hole past halfway without the whistle and the ash in his eyes

moves.doing: feeding his fire pit split sticks from the deadfall
moves.goal: keep a good bed of coals for the last of the peg hole

moves.doing: tending the fire pit, blowing a coal down the peg hole through the hollow stalk with short soft breaths
moves.goal: burn the hole the rest of the way through the split half

moves.doing: whittling a fat peg from a split stick with the long straight knife on the crate
moves.goal: make a peg thick enough to fill the too-wide top of the hole

moves.doing: checking the crayfish trap in the shallows by lantern
moves.goal: see whether anything walked in for tomorrow's tin

moves.doing: sketching the shed's sill and peg holes on the map sheet with the pencil by the lit grease lamp
moves.goal: work out how many peg holes the shed needs before he drives the first peg in daylight

moves.doing: whittling a second fat peg by his fire pit with the long straight knife
moves.goal: have pegs ready so daylight goes to driving them, not making them

moves.doing: checking the floating needle under the glass dome at the bench
moves.goal: make sure the needle still settles on its scratch, as he does every night

moves.doing: feeding his fire pit two split sticks from the deadfall laid crossways
moves.goal: keep his fire going until bed, since the last sticks were burning down to coals

moves.doing: carving a small starter pit into a fresh split half with the short stub knife at the bench
moves.goal: give tomorrow's coal a seat so the next hole starts where he wants it, not a finger too wide

moves.doing: eating the last apple from the food bundle on the crate
moves.goal: eat something before the cold hours, with the bundle nearly gone

moves.doing: carving a starter pit across the grain of a split half with the stub knife, the grease lamp burning beside it on the bench
moves.goal: cut a seat for tomorrow's coal that stays round instead of running into a slot

moves.doing: checking the stalk trap in the shallows by lantern light
moves.goal: see what the night has put in the pen, with only one breakfast of bundle left

moves.doing: feeding his fire pit one split stick from the deadfall
moves.goal: keep the fire going until bed and a little past, and get his creek-cold hands back

moves.doing: whittling a peg from a split half with the long knife by his fire pit
moves.goal: get a third peg ready for the sill boards while the fire is warm enough for his fingers

moves.doing: twisting gray stalk fiber into three-ply cord by his fire pit
moves.goal: have a spare fishing line before the bundle runs out tomorrow, in case another one parts

moves.doing: winding the spare toggle onto the new line with six tight turns at the bench
moves.goal: make the spare line ready to drop in the water at first light

moves.doing: checking the floating needle under the glass dome at the bench
moves.goal: make his nightly check that the needle still settles on its scratch

moves.doing: feeding his fire pit one thick split stick for the night
moves.goal: keep the fire going through the small hours now the sky has cleared and the cold is settling

moves.doing: sleeping on his bedroll under the wool blanket
moves.goal: sleep until first light, when the trap and two lines are waiting
